analysis.title: "This Is What I Got Wrong": Top Goldman Trader Flips On AI As Market Prices Peak CapEx...
key_insights: Goldman's Rich Privorotsky (head of EMEA 1-delta trading) said on Thursday 11/5 'This is what I got wrong' on AI: tech flows in Europe were overwhelmingly bearish, and the market is 'definitively pricing peak CapEx growth.' This follows his Monday note (nobody knows what to worry about) and Wednesday view that AI infrastructure was 'sold to death.'

The trigger is legislative restrictions: moratoria now threaten about 45% of planned US data center capacity. Building becomes more expensive, complicated and slower. Multiples have compressed and positioning was already de-risked before another wave of selling.

Goldman desks are pitching 'own the compute, sell the shovels.' Privorotsky says energised compute becomes more valuable, hyperscalers may get better economics on scarce capacity, and constrained expansion implies less CapEx and higher FCF. Scarcity is good for capacity owners and potentially bad for those whose valuations depend on building it.

John Flood (GS head of US execution services) says 'buying Hyperscalers vs Selling Semis' is the standout theme on the desk. His logic: scarce compute sells at a higher price, less capacity spending, and cash freed for buybacks. GS US Daily Download calls the backdrop good for hyperscalers and bad for neoclouds, semis and power, and that was the largest thematic on the desk's pad on Wednesday.

Privorotsky flags an inventory-cycle risk for the shovel sellers: delayed projects are not cancelled demand but could create a glut across chips, turbines, cooling and electrical equipment. He asks whether this undermines capacity expansion at ASML and TSMC. Newsquawk reports about 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips are piling up in Hong Kong awaiting Beijing import approval.

The article challenges the buyback thesis using GS GIR's 11/3 'What Matters Today': hyperscaler capex is about $800bn in 2026 (+96%) and expected at $1.2tn in 2027 (+44%) with little revision. AI infrastructure EPS growth is expected to peak at 80% this quarter and slow to about 40% by late 2027. Hyperscalers reported combined Q3 free cash flow of -$31bn.

Hyperscalers keep borrowing: Microsoft needed a $25bn bond deal after its beat and Meta raised $15bn on Tuesday. GS credit strategist Amanda Lynam estimates $1.7tn of hyperscaler lease commitments (75% not yet commenced) and $1.9tn of unconditional purchase commitments, $685bn due by year-end 2027.

Of $657bn of AI-related debt issued globally this year, hyperscalers account for $271bn (41%). The other 59% came from project finance, leveraged finance and AI-adjacent builders, sellers and power providers. The author argues the desk's two trades contradict each other: capped capacity hurts the debt-heavy rest of the complex, while uncapped capacity means capex keeps growing and there are no buybacks.

Earnings reaction data from GS strategy: the median S&P stock beating EPS has outperformed by 152bps the next day this season, TMT beats are rewarded with -76bps, and semis multiples fell from 28x to 16x in two months.
Index vol collapsed while single-name stress persisted: VIX -20% to 16.61 and VXN -18% to 25.08. Semiconductor vol (VXSMH) barely moved, leaving a gap of roughly 30 vol points (per The Market Ear).

Rotation into defensives: since earnings season began, 70% of S&P 500 stocks are up but represent only 50% of market cap, so the S&P is down 3% while the S&P ex-AI is up 5%. GS retail outperformed by 390bps on Wednesday, XLP hit an all-time high, and USMV broke out to a record $104.50.

GS Prime: fundamental L/S funds lost 3.5% and systematic L/S funds lost 3.6% in October, the first time since 2016 both fell 3% or more. Info Tech saw the largest net selling since June and defensives were net bought for the first time in seven months.

Positioning is light: global fundamental L/S net leverage is at the 3rd percentile on a one-year lookback and the 5th on three years, with the overall book at the 9th. Europe is the exception at the 68th percentile on three years. Privorotsky: 'nets are too low for the broader market to go down easily.'

Flood's midterm seasonality: since 1952, across 18 midterms the S&P averaged +7.5% through year end, +13.9% over six months and +15.5% over 12 months after the midterm, and was higher at both the six- and 12-month marks all 18 times.

Oil: Privorotsky says the unpopularity of the Iran war has eroded the oil risk premium. Physical Brent reportedly traded at a steep discount to Dated Brent and the swing is roughly $23 a barrel in three weeks. Some argue fair value is below $70. Brent's four-day drop is the worst since Covid.

Gold: Privorotsky calls it an inverse oil trade and says long gold is potentially a more defensible de-escalation trade than short oil, since EM central banks that sold gold to pay for energy stop selling as oil falls. The article notes WGC data shows central banks bought 321 tons in Q3 (+42% y/y), so forced sellers were a minority.
Escalation risk remains: the WSJ reported the US struck Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday and Tehran promised a 'far wider' response. Privorotsky asks whether there will be weekend escalation.

Flood says the most critical potential clearing event this year is tied to equity capital markets. The author expects the 'dry powder' to arrive as new bonds, SPVs and equity rather than buybacks. An Oracle offering reportedly needed an 11% discount, which Bloomberg's ECM desk says 'signals buyer fatigue.'

Privorotsky's bull path: energy normalizes, AI CapEx is rationalized rather than strangled, multiples have reflected the damage, and capital finds alternative jurisdictions and power solutions. He sees it as still supportive for equities even with AI in the backseat.

GS desk theme is selling semis versus buying hyperscalers. Semis multiples fell from 28x to 16x in two months and an inventory cycle is a risk.
GS US Daily Download says the political backdrop is bad for those who build out, sell into or power datacenters.
Staples hit an all-time high, USMV broke out, and defensives were net bought for the first time in seven months.

tension_points.bull_case: GS desks argue capped capacity makes existing compute scarcer, lifts pricing, cuts capex and frees cash for buybacks. Cloud revenue at Amazon, Google and Microsoft grew 54% y/y in Q3 and is still accelerating.
tension_points.bear_case: Hyperscalers had -$31bn Q3 FCF, capex is guided up 44% in 2027, and they carry $685bn of unconditional commitments due by end-2027. Microsoft and Meta are still issuing debt.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If capex keeps growing 44% next year, there are no buybacks. The bull case needs the moratoria to actually cut capex.

tension_points.bull_case: Fundamental L/S net leverage is at the 3rd percentile on a one-year lookback, so nets are too low for the market to go down easily. Midterm seasonality has been positive in all 18 cases.
tension_points.bear_case: The market is pricing peak capex growth, semis multiples fell from 28x to 16x, TMT beats are punished, and ECM supply is a pending clearing event.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A large equity capital markets supply wave, which Flood calls the most critical potential clearing event this year.

tension_points.bull_case: Oil is pricing the war as over, and long gold is a more defensible de-escalation trade than short oil because the forced central-bank selling stops.
tension_points.bear_case: A weekend escalation after the reported US strike on Qeshm Island and Tehran's promised 'far wider' response. Central banks bought 321 tons in Q3, so forced sellers were a minority.
